full_citation: Al-Qudsi, S. S., & Shah, N. M. (1991). The relative economic progress of male foreign workers in Kuwait. International Migration Review, 25(1), 141-166.
models_or_system: HUMAN labour market (observational earnings regressions on the 1983 Kuwait Labor Survey)
population_categories: Kuwait; male foreign workers in nine nationality groups (the nine groups are not named in the abstract)
manipulation: None (observational). Human-capital earnings functions with education, home and Kuwait-specific experience, occupation and ethnic background
outcome: Earnings and earnings growth with length of residence
main_result: HUMAN: economic progress with length of residence varies by education, experience, occupational status and ethnic background; 'about one third of the earnings inequality is due to unexplained factors including discrimination'. Which nationality groups rank at the top or bottom is not stated in the abstract
limitations: HUMAN; abstract only (SAGE and JSTOR paywalled); 1983 data, before the 1990-91 expulsions; men only; the unexplained share is a regression residual, not a direct measure of discrimination; group ranking not verified
relation_to_project: Closest peer-reviewed evidence found of earnings differences across several expatriate nationality groups inside a Gulf labour market with qualifications controlled; Kuwait is one of our eight base countries. Read the full text before citing any ranking or naming the groups

full_citation: Alfarhan, U. F., & Al-Busaidi, S. (2019). Migrant earnings gaps in Gulf Cooperation Council countries: Employers' perceptions or opportunity costs? International Labour Review, 158(2), 273-295.
models_or_system: HUMAN labour market (observational wage decomposition)
population_categories: GCC private sector, 2012-14; skilled migrants pooled into three groups: Western, Arab, Asian
manipulation: None (observational). Two standard decomposition methods
outcome: Real hourly earnings differentials between migrant groups
main_result: HUMAN: 'one-third to three-quarters of real hourly earnings differentials are attributable to differing observed levels of productivity-related characteristics'; the remainder is attributed to higher opportunity costs of Westerners in wage bargaining; unobserved employer perceptions are 'found to be irrelevant'
limitations: HUMAN; abstract only (Wiley paywalled); 'Arab' is one pooled category, so nothing on differences among Arab nationalities; data source and countries covered not stated in abstract
relation_to_project: Shows that Gulf wage research itself pools Arab expatriates into one category (Western / Arab / Asian). Part of the nationality pay gap is not explained by qualifications, but the authors attribute the residual to outside options, not to employer taste: a counterweight to a discrimination reading

full_citation: Gardner, A., Pessoa, S., Diop, A., Al-Ghanim, K., Le Trung, K., & Harkness, L. (2013). A portrait of low-income migrants in contemporary Qatar. Journal of Arabian Studies, 3(1), 1-17.
models_or_system: HUMAN labour market (representative survey of low-income migrants; SESRI sampling frame)
population_categories: Qatar; low-income migrant workers: Nepal 39%, India 29%, Sri Lanka 9%, Bangladesh 9%, Philippines 5%, Pakistan 3%, Egypt 3%. 'Arab' = primarily Egyptian plus a few Syrian
manipulation: None (observational survey, February-March 2012)
outcome: Basic monthly salary, migration cost, workdays per week, roommates, salary withholding
main_result: HUMAN: mean basic monthly salary Egypt QR1,454 and Philippines QR1,443 vs Nepal QR853 (lowest-earning nationality); Arab QR1,446 vs South Asian QR1,028; Arab migrants reported fewer workdays (5.87 vs 6.18 per week), fewer roommates and no salary withholding (0.0% vs 11.0%), but higher migration costs
limitations: HUMAN; descriptive means without controls for occupation or skill; 'only small numbers of Arab migrants'; 'Arab' is pooled (Egyptian plus a few Syrian), so no comparison among Arab nationalities; low-income segment only
relation_to_project: Peer-reviewed evidence of a nationality hierarchy in pay and treatment inside a base country (Qatar), with Arab workers above South Asian. Does not show differences among Arab origins and does not hold qualifications fixed

full_citation: Kapiszewski, A. (2006). Arab versus Asian migrant workers in the GCC countries (UN/POP/EGM/2006/02). United Nations Expert Group Meeting on International Migration and Development in the Arab Region, Beirut, 15-17 May 2006. United Nations Population Division.
venue: United Nations Population Division expert-group paper (GREY LITERATURE)
models_or_system: HUMAN (GCC governments, employers and nationals; narrative review of secondary statistics)
population_categories: Six GCC states; non-Gulf Arab expatriates (Egyptians, Yemenis, Palestinians/Jordanians, Sudanese, Syrians, Iraqis) vs Asian expatriates
manipulation: None (descriptive and historical review)
outcome: Composition of the foreign workforce; state and employer preferences; expulsions
main_result: HUMAN, GREY: Arab share of the GCC foreign population fell from 72% (1975) to 56% (1985) to 32% (2002/4) (Table 2); Asians 'were preferred to Arabs' as cheaper, easier to lay off and politically safer. Individual Arab nationalities were treated differently for political reasons: in 1990-91 'over 1.5 million people were expelled', incl. 'up to one million Yemenis' from Saudi Arabia, 200,000 Jordanians and 150,000 Palestinians; Qatar expelled about 700 Egyptian workers in 1996. Quotes Birks and Sinclair (1980): GCC nationals feel 'a detachment from Palestinians and Jordanians, a lack of respect for Yemenis, and mistrust and dislike of Egyptians'
limitations: HUMAN; grey literature, not peer-reviewed; figures are estimates from mixed secondary sources; the attitude statement is a secondary quotation from 1980 (original not located), not survey data; evidence concerns state policy and political events, not hiring with qualifications fixed; live UN URL returned 404 on 2026-10-04, read from a Wayback Machine capture
relation_to_project: Strongest located description of differential treatment of individual Arab nationalities inside the Gulf, driven by bilateral politics. Makes origin-specific effects plausible in our Gulf setting and supports the conflict/politics text flags. Does not measure hiring

full_citation: Razzaz, S. (2017). A challenging market becomes more challenging: Jordanian workers, migrant workers and refugees in the Jordanian labour market. Beirut: International Labour Organization, Regional Office for Arab States. ISBN 978-92-2-130340-4.
models_or_system: HUMAN employers and workers (structured interviews; secondary statistics)
population_categories: Jordan; Jordanians, migrant workers (largely Egyptian, also South Asian) and Syrian refugees; agriculture, construction, domestic work, manufacturing, tourism
manipulation: None (qualitative interviews)
sample_size: over 800 workers and unemployed people interviewed; over 100 key informants (per the acknowledgements)
outcome: Employer hiring preferences, working conditions, labour-market segmentation
main_result: HUMAN, GREY: 'Much of the segmentation is based not on education or initial skills but rather on nationality'; employers report 'high demand for Egyptian workers' for flexibility, long hours and tolerance of late pay; Syrians are described as accepting low wages but constrained by family duties and permit rules
limitations: HUMAN; grey literature; qualitative; executive summary and nationality passages read, not all 158 pages; no estimate with qualifications held fixed; the preference reflects legal status and bargaining position as much as origin stereotypes; low-skill sectors only
relation_to_project: Jordan is a base country. Documents sorting among Arab origins (Jordanian, Egyptian, Syrian) in a host Arab labour market. The channel is legal vulnerability, which our fixed work-authorisation line is meant to hold constant

full_citation: Abdulrahim, S., & Khawaja, M. (2011). The cost of being Palestinian in Lebanon. Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, 37(1), 151-166.
venue: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
models_or_system: HUMAN labour market (household survey, descriptive analysis)
population_categories: Lebanon; Palestinian refugees vs Lebanese in three low-income urban neighbourhoods of Beirut (2002 survey)
manipulation: None (observational)
outcome: Labour-force participation, occupational segregation, wages
main_result: HUMAN: Palestinian men are 'segregated into less-desirable segments of the mainstream economy and earn lower wages than Lebanese men in virtually all educational and occupational categories'; Palestinian women pay 'the highest cost in wages'
limitations: HUMAN; abstract only (tandfonline paywalled); descriptive; three neighbourhoods; exclusion is partly legal (restricted occupations), not only employer taste; Lebanon is not one of our base countries
relation_to_project: One Arab origin is paid less than host nationals within education and occupation cells in an Arab labour market. Legal exclusion is confounded with origin

full_citation: Al Ariss, A., & Guo, G. C. (2016). Job allocations as cultural sorting in a culturally diverse organizational context. International Business Review, 25(2), 579-588.
models_or_system: HUMAN managers (qualitative interviews)
population_categories: United Arab Emirates; Emirati and international employees in managerial positions
manipulation: None (qualitative)
outcome: Reported job-allocation practices
main_result: HUMAN: 'provides insights into the impact of cultural/nationality-based stereotypes on job allocations'; reports a lack of effective diversity management. Which nationalities are sorted into which jobs is not stated in the abstract
limitations: HUMAN; abstract only (read on the author's institutional repository page; ScienceDirect paywalled); qualitative, small sample; nationality detail not verified
relation_to_project: HRM evidence from a base country (UAE) that managers allocate jobs by nationality stereotype. Whether Arab nationalities are distinguished from each other is not verified

full_citation: Ewers, M. C., Gengler, J., & Shockley, B. (2021). Bargaining power: A framework for understanding varieties of migration experience. International Migration Review, 55(4), 1121-1151.
models_or_system: HUMAN (nationally representative survey of foreign residents)
population_categories: Qatar; 'a highly diverse sample of foreign residents'
manipulation: None (observational)
outcome: Typology of migration experience; life satisfaction; long-term settlement intentions
main_result: HUMAN: migrants' experience varies with individual cultural and socioeconomic capital and with the 'home country's political and physical security characteristics' (external bargaining power); both predict reported life satisfaction and settlement intentions
limitations: HUMAN; abstract only (SAGE paywalled); outcome is migrants' own experience, not employer decisions; nationality-level results not stated in abstract
relation_to_project: Supports origin-country characteristics, not a pooled region label, as what structures treatment in the Gulf: a human parallel to our exploratory origin-country moderators (H1d). Not a hiring outcome

full_citation: Shockley, B., & Gengler, J. J. (2024). Sharing citizenship: Economic competition, cultural threat, and immigration preferences in the rentier state. Political Science Research and Methods, 12(1), 59-75.
models_or_system: HUMAN citizens (survey experiments: choice task and conjoint; SESRI face-to-face survey)
population_categories: Qatar; Qatari citizens judging candidates for permanent residency; candidate nationalities drawn from common white-collar expatriate nationalities, from Yemeni (baseline, 'closest') to British ('furthest'); the full list is in the appendix (not read)
manipulation: Conjoint attributes: NATIONALITY, religion cued by first name (Sunni, Shi'i, Christian, or no name), language, salary, occupation, duration of residence; respondents could reject both candidates
outcome: Selection of a candidate for permanent residency
main_result: HUMAN: 'Qataris make no significant distinction ... between candidates of a diverse set of nationalities relative to the Yemeni baseline'; without a descent tie 'it matters very little whether they are nationals of a Western, South Asian, or Arab country'; descent-based claims dominate; monolingual Arabic speakers are preferred; lower-income citizens penalise the British nationality
limitations: HUMAN; outcome is permanent residency, not hiring; 733 respondents, so power for single nationality levels is limited; nationality list and effect sizes are in the appendix, not read; published online 2023
relation_to_project: NATIONALITY IS THE TREATMENT. The clearest located experiment inside a base country (Qatar) with applicant nationality randomised. The result for nationality is a null: evidence AGAINST differentiation among origins by Gulf citizens once other attributes are shown

full_citation: Blaydes, L., & Gengler, J. (2023). Arab identity and attitudes toward migration in Kuwait and Qatar. Research & Politics, 10(4).
models_or_system: HUMAN expatriate workers (online survey with framing experiment)
population_categories: Kuwait and Qatar; 2,941 expatriates: 2,731 Arab (Egyptian 1,129; Jordanian 405; Syrian 361; Sudanese 243; Lebanese 172; other Arab 421) and 210 non-Arab
manipulation: Framing experiment: priority for future migrants described as Arab or Indian, doctor or construction worker (ORIGIN GROUP IS A TREATMENT, at the pooled 'Arab' level)
outcome: Support for future migration; prioritisation of migrant types
main_result: HUMAN: 'Arab expatriates exhibit high levels of co-ethnic bias in favor of fellow Arabs, regardless of a prospective migrant's skill level' and disfavour Indian workers; Arab migrants are less supportive of future migration than non-Arab migrants
limitations: HUMAN; non-probability online sample, 93% Arab; the target is a pooled 'Arab' label, so differences among Arab nationalities as targets are not tested; attitudes, not hiring decisions; full text read from the author-posted PDF (SAGE returned 403)
relation_to_project: Arab expatriates in two base countries treat 'Arab' as one in-group against non-Arab migrants: support, from inside the region, for the pooled-category view. Says nothing about a hierarchy among Arab origins

full_citation: Barron, K., Harmgart, H., Huck, S., Schneider, S. O., & Sutter, M. (2023). Discrimination, narratives, and family history: An experiment with Jordanian host and Syrian refugee children. Review of Economics and Statistics, 105(4), 1008-1016.
models_or_system: HUMAN children (lab-in-the-field sharing experiment)
population_categories: Jordan; Jordanian host and Syrian refugee children aged 9-10 in 13 double-shift schools; Jordanian children with Palestinian roots analysed separately
manipulation: Group of the recipient (Jordanian vs Syrian) in two sharing tasks and one allocation task (NATIONALITY OF THE COUNTERPART IS THE TREATMENT)
outcome: Amount shared with in-group vs out-group recipients
main_result: HUMAN: 'only a small degree of out-group discrimination'; 'Jordanian children with Palestinian roots do not discriminate at all'; parents' narratives about the refugee crisis correlate with children's discrimination
limitations: HUMAN; children and sharing tasks, not employers or hiring; two groups only; results taken from the abstract; sample size and setting read in the accepted manuscript (MPG repository); results section and effect sizes not read
relation_to_project: One of the few experiments inside a base country (Jordan) where the counterpart's Arab nationality is randomised. Finds little discrimination between two Arab origins: evidence toward homogeneity, in a non-labour setting

full_citation: Krafft, C. (2025). Do employers discriminate against married women? Evidence from a field experiment in Egypt. Journal of Development Economics, 174, 103452.
models_or_system: HUMAN employers (correspondence audit)
population_categories: Egypt; fictitious applicants varying in gender and marital status; nationality NOT varied
manipulation: Gender and marital status on resumes sent to online job postings
outcome: Callback and type of employer response
main_result: HUMAN: 'More job postings explicitly required men (14 per cent) than women (4 per cent)'; callback differences by sex and marital status 'were not statistically significant'; women, especially married women, were more often asked for more information rather than scheduled for an interview
limitations: HUMAN; abstract only (read on RePEc; ScienceDirect paywalled); the treatment is gender and marital status, not nationality or origin
relation_to_project: Shows that correspondence audits are feasible in a base country (Egypt) and that job ads there state demographic requirements openly. No nationality treatment, so it does not answer our question. No correspondence audit with applicant nationality as the treatment was found for any Arab country

full_citation: Vernby, K., & Dancygier, R. (2019). Can immigrants counteract employer discrimination? A factorial field experiment reveals the immutability of ethnic hierarchies. PLoS ONE, 14(7), e0218044.
models_or_system: HUMAN employers (factorial correspondence experiment)
population_categories: Sweden; applicants born in Sweden, Poland, Iraq or Somalia (Iraq and Somalia are both Arab League members); restaurant and cafe jobs
manipulation: Country of birth stated on the CV (with first and last names common in the origin country), gender, citizenship, work experience, religious activity
outcome: Callback
main_result: HUMAN: callback 21% for native Swedes, 17% Poland, 10% Iraq, 5% Somalia; the Iraq vs Somalia difference is significant (p<.01); Somali-born men 2.5%; citizenship and experience did little to offset origin penalties
limitations: HUMAN; one low-skill sector; Somali applicants are plausibly read as Black African, so the Iraq-Somalia gap mixes national origin with race; only two Arab League origins
relation_to_project: Field evidence that two Arab League origins are treated very differently when origin is stated explicitly (country of birth on the CV), the same kind of cue as our Nationality line. Also a warning: Somalia, and by extension Sudan, Djibouti, Comoros and Mauritania, may act as a racial contrast rather than an 'Arab' one

full_citation: Ahmad, A. (2026). Does the name still matter? A longitudinal correspondence study of hiring discrimination by ethnicity and gender in a Nordic labour market. Canadian Review of Sociology, 63(2), e70040.
models_or_system: HUMAN employers (two correspondence experiments, 2016 and 2024)
population_categories: Finland; second-generation applicants with Finnish, English, Russian, Iraqi and Somali names
manipulation: Applicant name; the cover letter also states the mother tongue (e.g. Arabic, Somali) 'to further highlight ethnic background'
outcome: Callback
main_result: HUMAN: callbacks in 2016: Finnish 39.0%, English 26.9%, Russian 22.8%, Iraqi 13.4%, Somali 9.9%; in 2024: 41.6%, 30.3%, 22.1%, 20.2%, 16.8%. Iraqi is above Somali in both waves; penalties for both groups shrank significantly between waves
limitations: HUMAN; no direct Iraqi-vs-Somali significance test seen in the sections read; Somali plausibly read as Black African; one Arab-majority origin only. The 2016 wave was first reported in Ahmad (2020), Sociological Inquiry 90(3), 468-496, doi:10.1111/soin.12276 (abstract verified, not in the bib)
relation_to_project: Second Nordic audit placing Iraqi above Somali, consistent with vernby2019immigrants. The design needed an explicit mother-tongue line in addition to names to signal origin

full_citation: Bansak, K., Hainmueller, J., & Hangartner, D. (2016). How economic, humanitarian, and religious concerns shape European attitudes toward asylum seekers. Science, 354(6309), 217-222.
models_or_system: HUMAN public (conjoint survey experiment)
population_categories: 15 European countries; asylum-seeker profiles with origin Syria, Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Eritrea, Kosovo or Ukraine
manipulation: Nine randomised profile attributes, incl. country of origin and religion
outcome: Acceptance of the asylum seeker
main_result: HUMAN: 'the country of origin of an asylum-seeker plays only a minor role'; Kosovo least accepted, Syria and Ukraine most, with Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan and Eritrea in between; 'the maximum difference is only 4 percentage points'; Muslim asylum seekers are 'about 11 percentage points less likely to be accepted' than otherwise similar Christians
limitations: HUMAN; asylum admission, not hiring; only two Arab origins (Syria, Iraq); the 2016 context favoured Syrians; read in the accepted manuscript (LSE Research Online)
relation_to_project: Large-N evidence on both sides: Syria and Iraq are told apart (Syria preferred), but the origin effect is small next to religion. Predicts modest within-Arab dispersion once other attributes are specified, and religion as the dominant channel ('Muslim by default')

full_citation: Hainmueller, J., & Hopkins, D. J. (2015). The hidden American immigration consensus: A conjoint analysis of attitudes toward immigrants. American Journal of Political Science, 59(3), 529-548.
models_or_system: HUMAN public (conjoint survey experiment)
population_categories: United States; immigrant profiles with nine attributes incl. country of origin (the list of origins is not in the abstract)
manipulation: Nine randomised immigrant attributes
sample_size: not stated in abstract (two-wave population-based survey)
outcome: Support for admission
main_result: HUMAN: Americans view unfavourably immigrants who 'lack plans to work, entered without authorization, are Iraqi, or do not speak English'; preferences vary little with respondents' education, partisanship or ethnocentrism
limitations: HUMAN; abstract only (Wiley paywalled; no open copy reachable); effects for other origins are not stated in the abstract; immigration admission, not hiring
relation_to_project: A single Arab origin (Iraqi) is singled out for a penalty in a design with many origins. Same task type as mao2025gatekeepers (LLM); whether Mao and Zhao replicate this design was not verified

full_citation: Valfort, M.-A. (2020). Anti-Muslim discrimination in France: Evidence from a field experiment. World Development, 135, 105022.
models_or_system: HUMAN employers (correspondence audit)
population_categories: France; applicants who emigrated from Lebanon, of Muslim vs Christian culture (plus Jewish), religious vs non-religious
manipulation: Religion and religiosity (via the type of scouting association), with NATIONAL ORIGIN HELD CONSTANT (Lebanon)
outcome: Callback
main_result: HUMAN: with Lebanese origin held constant, callback 11.7% for applicants of Muslim culture vs 18.4% for Christian (6.7 percentage points); non-religious Muslims 12.9% vs non-religious Christians 16.1% (not significant); religious Muslim men 4.7% vs religious Christian men 17.9%
limitations: HUMAN; numbers read in the working-paper version (IZA DP 11417, 2018). The journal abstract, as recorded by the parallel part L3 (same key), gives different figures for religious men (4.2% vs 10.9%), so the working-paper numbers must not be cited as the published result; one Arab origin only; no native-French comparator; France
relation_to_project: Separates 'Arab origin' from 'Muslim': within one Arab nationality, religion signals drive a large gap. A nationality line that implies a different religious make-up could therefore produce origin gaps through religion. Bears on the Arab-Muslim conflation in bartkoski2018meta

full_citation: Mathews, K., Phelan, J., Jones, N. A., Konya, S., Marks, R., Pratt, B. M., Coombs, J., & Bentley, M. (2017). 2015 National Content Test: Race and ethnicity analysis report. Washington, DC: U.S. Census Bureau.
venue: U.S. Census Bureau report (official methodology; GREY LITERATURE)
models_or_system: HUMAN respondents (split-sample questionnaire experiment)
population_categories: United States; working MENA classification of 19 nationalities (Algerian, Bahraini, Egyptian, Emirati, Iraqi, Iranian, Israeli, Jordanian, Kuwaiti, Lebanese, Libyan, Moroccan, Omani, Palestinian, Qatari, Saudi Arabian, Syrian, Tunisian, Yemeni) plus ethnic groups; Somali, Sudanese, Mauritanian and Djiboutian are outside it
manipulation: Questionnaire with vs without a distinct 'Middle Eastern or North African' category
outcome: Self-reported race/ethnicity category
main_result: HUMAN: with a MENA category, 'people who identified as MENA predominantly reported in the MENA category'; Jordanians 94.4% in MENA; over 90% for Egyptians, Iraqis, Jordanians, Libyans, Palestinians, Saudi Arabians and Yemenis; but 34.0% of Lebanese still reported White (Egyptians 8.4%); Somali respondents chose MENA 0.0% (94.2% Black) and Sudanese 8.0% (87.2% Black). Experts disagreed on whether Turkey, Sudan or Somalia belong in MENA
limitations: HUMAN; self-identification in the US, not how employers perceive applicants; small cells for some nationalities; Somali was shown as an example under the Black category in all questionnaire designs, which the report says may have affected Somali reporting; only the executive summary and section 5.2 were read
relation_to_project: Official evidence that one MENA category fits the self-identification of most Arab-origin groups, and where it breaks: Arab League members Somalia and Sudan fall outside it and Lebanese partly so. Our 22-nationality Arab League set is wider than the perceptual 'Arab/MENA' category

full_citation: Office of Management and Budget. (2024). Revisions to OMB's Statistical Policy Directive No. 15: Standards for maintaining, collecting, and presenting federal data on race and ethnicity. Federal Register, 89, 22182-22196 (29 March 2024), document 2024-06469.
venue: Federal Register notice (official standard; GREY LITERATURE)
models_or_system: OFFICIAL STANDARD (no subjects of its own; relies on HUMAN respondent tests such as mathews2017national)
population_categories: United States federal race and ethnicity categories
manipulation: None (standard-setting notice)
outcome: Category definitions and collection rules
main_result: Adds 'Middle Eastern or North African' as a minimum reporting category separate from White, defined as origins 'including, for example, Lebanese, Iranian, Egyptian, Syrian, Iraqi, and Israeli'; the six MENA checkboxes are Lebanese, Syrian, Egyptian, Moroccan, Iranian and Israeli; 'agencies are required to collect the detailed categories described in this Notice as a default'; Somali and Sudanese are left out because most such respondents 'did not select MENA when it was offered' in the 2015 test
limitations: Official notice, not a study; US context; the category mixes Arab and non-Arab origins (Iranian, Israeli)
relation_to_project: An institutional precedent for our framing: a pooled label is adopted and disaggregation by nationality is required by default. Confirms that MENA is neither 'Arab' nor 'Arab League'
novelty_threat_reason: Official statistical standard, not an LLM study

full_citation: Maghbouleh, N., Schachter, A., & Flores, R. D. (2022). Middle Eastern and North African Americans may not be perceived, nor perceive themselves, to be White. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 119(7), e2117940119.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
models_or_system: HUMAN perceivers and self-identifiers (two online survey experiments: external-classification conjoint; self-identification)
population_categories: United States; non-MENA White and MENA respondents; profile ancestries grouped as Middle Eastern Arab (Lebanese and Syrian ancestors), North African and Iranian
manipulation: Conjoint of ancestry, name, religion, language, skin colour and occupation; MENA response option offered or not
sample_size: 421 non-Hispanic White respondents (4 excluded); 333 MENA respondents via Prolific (330 analysed) plus a second MENA sample via Lucid (size not extracted)
outcome: Classification of profiles as MENA, White or Black; self-identification
main_result: HUMAN: both groups classify MENA traits as MENA rather than White; a fully Arab ancestry raises MENA classification by 36 percentage points among White and 51 among MENA respondents; MENA names and languages add 5 to 20 points; Muslim adds 8 to 11 points; 88% of MENA respondents chose MENA when offered; 12% of North African-ancestry respondents identified as exclusively Black vs 1% of Middle Eastern
limitations: HUMAN; non-probability online samples; North Africans under-represented; ancestry is varied in regional bundles, so the study cannot show whether perceivers tell Arab nationalities apart
relation_to_project: Outsiders apply one MENA category across Arab, North African and Iranian cues, which is the pooling our introduction describes; religion is an additive cue. Does not test within-Arab distinctions

full_citation: Martiniello, B., & Verhaeghe, P.-P. (2022). Signaling ethnic-national origin through names? The perception of names from an intersectional perspective. PLoS ONE, 17(8), e0270990.
models_or_system: HUMAN perceivers (name-perception survey)
population_categories: Belgium (Flanders); 180 names of Belgian, Moroccan, Turkish, Polish and Congolese origin, homogeneous and mixed
manipulation: Names rated for ethnic-national origin, gender, religiosity, social class and education
outcome: Congruence between perceived and intended origin
main_result: HUMAN: 'respondents distinguish Belgian from non-Belgian names rather than perceiving a specific ethnic-national origin'; non-Belgian names are recognised as non-Belgian at about 95.5% (mixed) to 98.5% (homogeneous), but only 48.2% of homogeneous Moroccan names are identified as non-European and 34% are assigned to Morocco (Turkish names: 34.5% to Turkey); homogeneous Moroccan and Turkish names are mostly perceived as religious (45.8% and 40.6%)
limitations: HUMAN; Flanders only; one Arab origin (Moroccan), so confusion among Arab nationalities is not measured directly; what Moroccan names were mistaken for was not extracted; Table 1 is row-shifted in the text extraction, so only figures confirmed in the running text are quoted
relation_to_project: Direct support for the methodological point in our introduction: names signal 'foreign' and 'Muslim', not a specific country, so name-based audits cannot separate Arab national origins. Justifies the explicit Nationality line

full_citation: Mubarak, H., & Darwish, K. (2015). Classifying Arab names geographically. In Proceedings of the Second Workshop on Arabic Natural Language Processing (pp. 1-8). Association for Computational Linguistics.
venue: Second Workshop on Arabic Natural Language Processing (ACL-IJCNLP 2015)
models_or_system: Naive Bayes and SVM name classifiers (NOT an LLM; NOT human perceivers)
population_categories: Arabic Twitter user names with self-declared location; 18 of the 22 Arab countries (no Arabic tweets found for Mauritania, Somalia, Djibouti, Comoros); regions: Gulf (incl. Iraq), Egypt, Levant, Maghreb, other
manipulation: None (supervised classification)
sample_size: about 1 million unique user names mapped to Arab countries
outcome: Accuracy of predicting country and region from the name
main_result: Names in Arabic script: 79% country and 94% region accuracy, against majority-class baselines of 74.2% and 91.4% (93% of Arabic-script names come from the Gulf). Transliterated names: 67% country and 83% region accuracy against baselines of 44.3% and 67.4%
limitations: A machine classifier on full user names (family and tribal names carry much of the signal), not human perception; small gain over baseline for Arabic-script names; self-declared Twitter locations
relation_to_project: Counter-evidence to 'Arabic names carry no origin signal': full names in Latin script do carry country and especially regional information for a trained model, so an LLM could infer region from a surname. Our no-name design closes this channel
novelty_threat_reason: Pre-LLM name classifier; no hiring or bias outcome

full_citation: Ye, J., Han, S., Hu, Y., Coskun, B., Liu, M., Qin, H., & Skiena, S. (2017). Nationality classification using name embeddings. In Proceedings of the 2017 ACM Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM '17) (pp. 1897-1906). ACM.
models_or_system: NamePrism name-embedding classifier (NOT an LLM; NOT human perceivers)
population_categories: 39 leaf 'nationality' groups covering 118 countries. Arab countries fall into three leaves under a 'Muslim' node: ArabianPeninsula (UAE, Iraq, Yemen, Bahrain, Syria, Jordan, Oman, Lebanon, Qatar, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia), Maghreb (Tunisia, Morocco, Algeria, Libya), Nubian (Egypt, Somalia, Sudan)
manipulation: None (supervised classification)
outcome: F1 of name-based nationality classification
main_result: The 'fine-grained' taxonomy does not separate individual Arab countries: eleven Gulf, Levant and Iraq countries form one leaf; F1 of 0.795 on 13 common classes (abstract)
limitations: The taxonomy is a design choice by the authors, informed by name similarity, not a test of whether Arab countries can be separated; machine, not human; read in the arXiv version (1708.07903)
relation_to_project: A standard name-to-origin tool used in social science pools Arab names into at most three clusters, one reason name-based audits and data pipelines report a single 'Arab' or 'Muslim' group. Read with mubarak2015classifying, which shows more signal is recoverable
novelty_threat_reason: Pre-LLM name classifier; no hiring or bias outcome
